cards.title: The Microservices Testing Pyramid
cards.teaser: Mike Cohn's classic test pyramid still applies to microservices — but the distribution shifts: more contract tests, far fewer end-to-end tests, and a new layer for component tests that did not exist in the monolith era.

runs.text: The original test pyramid (Cohn, 2009) prescribes many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and the smallest possible number of UI/E2E tests. The rationale is speed and isolation: tests near the bottom run in milliseconds; tests at the top can take minutes and fail for reasons unrelated to the code under test.
In a microservices system, the pyramid is adapted:

explanation.code:
/\
         /E2\
        / E  \   <-- tiny: full system, real network
       /------\
      /Compon- \
     / ent     \  <-- service in isolation, stubs at boundary
    /------------\
   /  Contract   \  <-- consumer-driven, replaces many E2E
  /----------------\
 /   Integration    \ <-- DB, broker, real infra, no network hops
/--------------------\
       Unit           <-- largest layer, pure logic, no I/O

runs.text: Key differences from the monolith pyramid:

items.text: Contract tests

are promoted to a first-class layer. In a monolith, service boundaries are internal — they can be refactored freely. In microservices, they are network interfaces that independent teams own, and breakage is expensive.
Component tests
emerge as a distinct layer: test a single deployable service end-to-end but replace all its collaborators with test doubles. This fills the gap between unit and full-system E2E.
E2E tests shrink dramatically.
With contract tests covering inter-service contracts and component tests covering service behavior, E2E tests can focus on the narrowest set of critical user journeys — typically fewer than a dozen.

runs.text: Sam Newman (Building Microservices) and Toby Clemson ("Testing Strategies in a Microservice Architecture") both argue that the E2E suite should be treated as a last resort, not a safety net. Contract tests and component tests are cheaper, faster, and more actionable.

The testing pyramid still holds in microservices — lots of unit tests at the bottom, very few E2E tests at the top — but two new layers appear in the middle: contract tests that verify service boundaries, and component tests that test one service in isolation with fake neighbors.

cards.title: Unit Tests in Microservices
cards.teaser: Unit tests are the fastest, most plentiful, and most isolated tests in the suite. In a microservices codebase they focus on domain logic, command handlers, and event transformations — pure functions with no I/O.

runs.text: A unit test exercises a single class or function in process, with all dependencies replaced by fakes or stubs. No network, no database, no message broker — just the logic under test and the data it needs.
In a microservices architecture the richest targets for unit tests are:

items.text: Domain entities and value objects
— the business rules encoded in the domain model (e.g., Order.cancel() throws if the order is already shipped).
Command handlers and application services
— the orchestration logic that drives domain objects and emits events, with repositories and message publishers stubbed.
Event transformations
— functions that map from one event schema to another, or from raw database records to domain events.
Validation and parsing logic
— input validation, schema coercion, and error message generation.

runs.text: The defining characteristic of a unit test is speed: a full unit suite for a microservice should run in seconds, not minutes. This allows developers to run the suite on every file save during local development, closing the inner loop as tightly as possible.

A common mistake is writing unit tests for infrastructure code — the HTTP handler wiring, the database query builder, the message serializer. These belong in integration tests. Unit-testing infrastructure gives false confidence: the test passes but the real wiring is broken.
Unit tests check pure logic: business rules, transformations, validation. They run in-process with no network or database. Fast enough to run on every file save.

cards.title: Integration Tests — Real Infra, No Network Hops
cards.teaser: Integration tests verify that a service talks correctly to its own infrastructure — its database, its message broker, its cache. They use real infra (via Docker containers) but no other services across the network.

runs.text: The word "integration" is overloaded. In the microservices testing pyramid it has a specific, narrow meaning: tests that exercise the integration between one service and one piece of infrastructure it owns, in isolation from all other services.
What a microservices integration test covers:

items.text: Repository tests
— a real PostgreSQL instance (spun up via Testcontainers or Docker Compose) receives the queries the repository class generates. Verifies SQL, index usage, transaction isolation.
Message broker tests
— a real Kafka or RabbitMQ instance receives a published event and the consumer logic reads it back. Verifies serialization, topic routing, consumer group offsets.
External HTTP client tests
— if a service calls a third-party API directly (not another internal microservice), this is integration-tested against a local WireMock stub of that API.

runs.text: Testcontainers (Java, Go, Python, .NET) has become the standard tool for spinning up real database and broker instances for integration tests. It starts a Docker container before the test suite, runs tests against it, and tears it down after. CI pipelines run Docker-in-Docker or use a remote Docker daemon to support this pattern.

Integration tests should not call other microservices over the network. Cross-service behavior is the domain of contract tests and component tests. Mixing the two makes integration tests slow, fragile, and hard to parallelize.
Integration tests use a real database or real broker — started in Docker — but talk only to that one piece of infrastructure. No other services, no network calls to neighbors.

cards.title: Contract Testing — The Core Idea
cards.teaser: A contract test captures the agreement between two services: the consumer says what it needs, the provider says what it offers, and a pact verifies they match. It replaces the most fragile inter-service E2E tests with fast, targeted assertions.

runs.text: When Service A calls Service B, two parties must agree on the shape of the API: the request format, the response schema, the status codes, and the error contracts. Without a formal agreement, this implicit contract drifts silently. Service B ships a breaking change; Service A discovers it in production.
Contract testing makes the agreement explicit and machine-verifiable. A
contract
is a document that specifies the interactions a consumer expects from a provider. It describes requests and their expected responses in enough detail to run as automated tests against both sides.
The test flow:

items.text: The consumer team writes tests that describe the interactions they rely on. These tests run against a mock provider and produce a contract file.
The contract file is published to a shared broker (the Pact Broker).
The provider team runs the contract as a verification suite against their real service. If the provider's responses match the contract, verification passes.
Both sides run verification on every CI pipeline. A failed contract verification blocks the build before any deployment happens.

runs.text: The result: a breaking change in the provider is caught in the provider's own CI pipeline, before it reaches staging, before it causes an integration failure, and with a clear signal about which consumer is affected.

Contract testing is not a replacement for all E2E testing. It verifies that the contract is honored — not that the business logic behind the contract is correct. It sits below component tests in the pyramid, not above them.

A contract test is a formal record of what a consumer expects from a provider. Both sides test against it independently. If the provider changes the API in a breaking way, the contract test fails in the provider's CI before anyone deploys anything broken.

cards.title: Consumer-Driven Contracts with Pact
cards.teaser: Pact is the dominant consumer-driven contract testing framework. The consumer writes the test, Pact records the interaction into a JSON pact file, and the provider runs that file as a verification suite — reversing the traditional testing responsibility.

runs.text: Pact (pact.io) implements the consumer-driven contract (CDC) pattern. The key insight: the consumer knows what it needs; the provider knows what it offers. Letting the consumer write the contract closes the gap. The provider cannot accidentally break the consumer if the consumer's expectations are encoded as executable tests.
A minimal Pact interaction (the JSON contract file published to the broker):
Key elements:

items.text: matchingRules
allow type-based matching rather than exact value matching. The consumer does not care that
quantityOnHand
is exactly 150 — it cares that it is a number.
The pact file is version-controlled and shared via the
Pact Broker
(open source or PactFlow SaaS), which also tracks which provider versions have verified which consumer versions.
Can-I-Deploy
is the Pact CLI command that queries the broker to answer: "Is it safe to deploy this consumer version against this provider version?" It gates promotion in the pipeline.

runs.text: Pact supports HTTP/REST (Pact V2/V3), gRPC (via plugin), and message contracts for async events. The message contract format is identical structurally but describes the event payload shape rather than an HTTP request/response pair.

Pact works like this: the consumer writes a test that records what it expects from the provider. That record becomes a JSON file. The provider then runs that JSON file against itself to prove it still honors the contract. If the provider changes something the consumer needs, the test fails.

cards.title: Spring Cloud Contract — Server-Side CDC
cards.teaser: Spring Cloud Contract inverts the Pact model: the provider defines the contract, generates a stub from it, and ships the stub to the consumer. Strong in Spring ecosystems; the provider retains ownership of the contract definition.

runs.text: Spring Cloud Contract (SCC) is the primary CDC tool in the Spring/Java ecosystem. It takes a different ownership model than Pact:

items.text: Pact (consumer-driven):
The consumer team writes the contract. The contract is a statement of consumer needs. The provider verifies against it.
Spring Cloud Contract (provider-driven):

The provider team writes the contract in a Groovy or YAML DSL. SCC generates: (1) acceptance tests that run against the provider, and (2) a WireMock stub JAR that consumers add to their test classpath.

runs.text: A Spring Cloud Contract DSL stub definition:

The trade-off: SCC integrates deeply with the Spring ecosystem (MockMvc, RestAssured, WebTestClient) and requires no separate broker infrastructure. But provider-driven contracts can drift from real consumer needs if consumers do not actively participate in reviewing the contract definitions.

In practice, many teams use both: Pact for cross-team contracts between teams that do not share a codebase or framework, and Spring Cloud Contract for intra-team contracts within a Java monorepo or tightly coupled Spring microservices.

Spring Cloud Contract works in reverse from Pact: the provider writes the contract definition, and the tool generates both the provider's tests and a stub the consumer can use in its own tests. Good for Spring shops; less consumer-driven than Pact.

cards.title: Provider-Side Contract Verification
cards.teaser: Provider verification is the other half of CDC: the provider's CI pipeline fetches contracts from the broker, replays each interaction against the real service, and publishes the result. A failed verification blocks the provider from deploying.

runs.text: Publishing a contract is only half the work. For CDC to provide safety, the provider must run the consumer's expectations against its real implementation on every build.
The provider verification flow in CI:

items.text: The provider's CI pipeline starts the service locally (or points at a test instance).
Pact fetches all contracts from all registered consumers from the Pact Broker.
For each interaction in each contract, Pact replays the recorded request against the running provider and compares the actual response to the expected response.
Results (pass/fail per interaction) are published back to the broker with the provider version tag.
The pipeline queries
can-i-deploy
before promoting the artifact. Deployment is blocked if any consumer contract is not verified for the current version.

runs.text: Provider state setup is a critical implementation detail. If an interaction requires the provider to have specific data (e.g., item 42 must exist), the consumer declares a
provider state
string (e.g., "item 42 exists"). The provider implements a state setup endpoint that Pact calls before replaying each interaction to seed the required data.

Provider state setup is where most Pact implementations become brittle. Keep provider states coarse-grained ("an item exists") rather than fine-grained ("item 42 with quantityOnHand 150 exists"). Fine-grained states create a maintenance burden and couple the consumer's test to provider internals.

Provider verification runs the consumer's recorded expectations against the real provider service in CI. If the provider's response no longer matches what the consumer expects, the build fails — before the provider deploys anything.

cards.title: Component Tests — One Service, Stubbed Neighbors
cards.teaser: A component test deploys one service with its real database but replaces all downstream services with stubs. It verifies the service's complete behavior — HTTP surface, persistence, event emission — without depending on any live neighbor.

runs.text: Component tests occupy the layer between integration tests (one service + its own infra) and E2E tests (full system). The service under test is started with its full dependency stack — real database, real message broker, real configuration — but all calls to other microservices are intercepted by WireMock or Mountebank stubs.
What component tests verify:

items.text: The complete HTTP surface of the service:
request routing, middleware, authentication, serialization, error handling.
The full business flow through the service:
a POST to the API triggers domain logic, writes to the database, and emits an event to the broker.
Resilience behavior:
what happens when a stubbed downstream service returns a 503? Does the service circuit-break correctly?
Configuration correctness:
environment variables, feature flags, and secrets are wired up correctly to the application.

runs.text: Component tests are more expensive than unit tests (they start a real service process) but far cheaper than E2E tests (no network dependencies, deterministic stub behavior, parallelizable across services). A component suite typically runs in 1-5 minutes.

In the "testing honeycomb" (Martin Fowler) framing, component tests are the widest middle layer, not the narrowest. For microservices, this shape — thin at E2E, wide at component — is often a better fit than the classic pyramid because each service is small enough to test meaningfully in isolation.

A component test runs the full service — real database, real broker — but replaces every other microservice with a fake. It tests the service as a whole without depending on the rest of the system being available.

cards.title: End-to-End Tests — the Expensive Apex
cards.teaser: E2E tests deploy the full system and exercise it through real interfaces. They provide the highest confidence but pay for it with slow execution, environmental fragility, non-deterministic failures, and difficult root-cause analysis.

runs.text: An end-to-end test starts every service, all their databases, all their brokers, and all their external dependencies — in a real or realistic environment — and exercises a user-visible flow from the outside. It is the most realistic test, and the most expensive.
The costs of E2E tests in a microservices system are amplified relative to a monolith:

items.text: Setup complexity scales with service count.
Ten services means ten databases to seed, ten containers to start, ten health checks to wait on. Docker Compose or Kubernetes-in-CI helps but does not eliminate the complexity.
Flakiness accumulates multiplicatively.
If each service has a 1% flakiness rate and ten services are involved, the test has a ~10% chance of failing for reasons unrelated to the code being tested.
Failures are hard to attribute.
A failed E2E test says "the system is broken" but not which service, which code path, or which team owns the fix.
Environment sharing creates contention.
When multiple teams share an E2E environment, a bad deploy by one team blocks every other team's tests.

runs.text: Best practice: maintain a small, stable set of E2E tests (fewer than 20) covering the most critical user journeys — checkout, authentication, payment. Invest in contract tests and component tests to reduce reliance on E2E tests for catching regressions.

The "all green, then deploy" discipline breaks down for E2E tests in large microservices systems. Teams often find themselves maintaining a "known flaky" list and checking if failures are "real." When this pattern emerges, it is a signal that the E2E suite has grown beyond its manageable size.

E2E tests run the full system and test real flows. They give the most confidence but are slow, flaky, hard to debug, and scale badly with the number of services. Keep the E2E suite small and rely on contract tests and component tests for most coverage.

cards.title: Service Virtualization — WireMock and Mountebank
cards.teaser: Service virtualization uses a stub server to stand in for unavailable or slow dependencies. WireMock excels in JVM environments; Mountebank is polyglot and protocol-agnostic. Both enable fast, deterministic testing without live neighbors.

runs.text: Service virtualization is the practice of replacing a real service dependency with a configurable simulator for test purposes. The stub server listens on the same port and protocol as the real service but returns pre-programmed responses.
The two dominant tools:

items.text: WireMock

(wiremock.io) — HTTP stub server written in Java. Deep integration with JUnit and Spring Boot. Can record real traffic and replay it. Supports response templating, fault injection (connection reset, chunked response, latency injection), and stateful scenarios. Available as a standalone JAR, Docker image, or embedded library. Pact uses WireMock internally to serve consumer contract stubs during consumer tests.
Mountebank

(mbtest.org) — polyglot stub server. Speaks HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, and SMTP. Configured via REST API or JSON files. Language-agnostic — a Node.js service, a Go service, and a Python service can all point to the same Mountebank instance in a component test. Supports injection (JavaScript response functions), which enables stateful behavior more flexibly than WireMock scenarios.

runs.text: A WireMock stub definition:
Service virtualization enables:

items.text: Testing in parallel across teams
— Team A can test against a stub of Team B's service while Team B is still building it.
Reproducible failure scenarios
— inject 5xx errors, timeouts, and malformed responses deterministically to test resilience paths.
Cost reduction
— avoid calling third-party APIs (payment processors, SMS gateways) in every test run.

runs.text: WireMock and Mountebank are stub servers — they pretend to be real services, return pre-configured responses, and let you test your service's behavior in isolation. WireMock is JVM-native; Mountebank works for any language and protocol.

cards.title: Test Data Management
cards.teaser: Shared test databases, state leakage between tests, and the fixture maintenance problem are the most common causes of flaky integration and component tests. Good test data management uses isolated databases, factories over fixtures, and teardown-first strategies.

runs.text: Test data management is harder in microservices than in monoliths because data is partitioned across service-owned databases. Each service's tests must manage their own data independently — there is no shared schema to reset between tests.
Key principles:

items.text: Database per test run, not per test suite.
Using Testcontainers, spin up a fresh database per test class or per CI run. Prevents state leakage between parallel test pipelines.
Factories over fixtures.
A test factory creates minimal, valid objects programmatically (e.g.,
OrderFactory.build(status: 'pending')
). Fixtures are static JSON/SQL files that accumulate and drift. Factories stay in sync with the model because they use the same constructors.
Teardown-first.
Delete test data at the start of each test rather than at the end. If a prior test crashed before cleanup, teardown-first prevents poisoned state from failing the next test.
Avoid the shared test database.
A single staging database shared across all tests is a deadlock waiting to happen. Tests step on each other's data, parallelism is impossible, and flakiness is guaranteed.

runs.text: The test data sharing problem emerges when E2E tests must involve data across service boundaries. Service A creates an order; Service B needs to fulfill it. There is no shared database to seed — the data must flow through the real APIs. This is expensive. Component tests avoid this by stubbing the data at the API boundary.

Avoid test data that depends on real external IDs (e.g., a specific product ID that must exist in production). Tests that depend on production data become brittle when production data changes. Generate synthetic IDs in tests and stub the lookups.

Test data management means giving each test run its own clean database, building test objects with factories rather than static files, and deleting test data before tests run — not after. Shared test databases always become a source of flakiness.

cards.title: Testing Async and Event-Driven Flows
cards.teaser: Event-driven systems are hard to test because cause and effect are decoupled in time. The service publishes an event; another service processes it eventually. "Eventually" does not work in a test suite that expects deterministic, synchronous assertions.

runs.text: In a synchronous microservice, a test can call the API and assert the response immediately. In an event-driven system, publishing an event is the output — the downstream effect may happen milliseconds or seconds later, in another process.
Strategies for testing async flows:

items.text: Test the publisher and consumer independently.

The publisher test verifies that the correct event was emitted to the broker (using an embedded broker or WireMock's message stubbing). The consumer test feeds a known event into the consumer and asserts the resulting state change. No actual async flow required.
Pact message contracts.

Pact supports message interactions. The consumer declares what event payload it expects to receive; the provider verifies it emits a payload matching that schema. No broker needed — both sides test against the same contract JSON.
Polling with timeout.
In component or E2E tests that must cross the async boundary, poll for the expected state change with a timeout and backoff. Awaitility (Java) and similar libraries provide readable polling DSLs.
Event spy.

Subscribe a test consumer to the broker topic. After triggering the action, wait for the spy to receive the expected event and assert its payload. This keeps the assertion deterministic while testing the real publish path.

runs.text: Thread.sleep() in async tests is a code smell. Fixed sleeps make tests slow in the success case and flaky when the system is under load and takes longer than the sleep. Use polling with a timeout instead.

Testing async flows means splitting the publisher and consumer into separate tests — each tested against the event contract — rather than trying to test the full async journey in one test. When you must cross the async boundary, poll for the expected outcome with a timeout.

cards.title: Testing in Production — Synthetic Monitoring
cards.teaser: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted, fake user flows against production at regular intervals. It detects regressions that only appear in the live environment — third-party API changes, CDN issues, certificate expiry — before real users notice.

runs.text: Testing in production is not a substitute for pre-production testing — it is an acknowledgment that some problems only manifest in production: real traffic patterns, real infrastructure, real third-party behavior.
The primary techniques:

items.text: Synthetic monitoring

— a scheduled agent (Datadog Synthetics, New Relic Synthetics, AWS CloudWatch Canaries) executes scripted API calls or browser flows against production every 1-5 minutes. Alerts fire when assertions fail. This is the closest equivalent to running your E2E test suite continuously against production.
Dark launches

— a new code path is deployed and executed for real production traffic, but its results are discarded. The response the user receives comes from the old code path. Used to validate that the new path runs without errors at production scale before switching over.
Shadow traffic

— real production requests are duplicated (shadowed) to a new service version. Both versions process the request; only the primary's response is returned to the user. The shadow's responses are compared to the primary's to detect behavioral divergence.
A/B testing and canary analysis

— a percentage of production traffic is routed to the new version. Automated canary analysis (Spinnaker, Argo Rollouts) compares error rates, latency, and business metrics between the old and new versions. Automatic rollback fires if the canary degrades.

runs.text: Testing in production requires investment in observability: structured logging, distributed tracing, and metrics must be in place before these techniques are useful. Without observability, you can detect that something broke but not diagnose where or why.

Synthetic monitoring runs fake user flows against real production on a schedule, catching problems that only show up in the live environment. Dark launches and shadow traffic let you test new code with real load without exposing users to the results.

cards.title: Chaos Testing — Failure Injection
cards.teaser: Chaos testing deliberately injects failures — killed processes, saturated networks, corrupted responses — into a running system to discover resilience gaps before a real outage does. Principles Engine is the discipline; Chaos Monkey is the first famous tool.

runs.text: Chaos engineering, formalized by Netflix and codified in the Principles of Chaos Engineering (principlesofchaos.org), treats a distributed system as a subject of scientific experiment. The hypothesis is: "The system remains available under failure condition X." The experiment injects X and observes whether the hypothesis holds.
Common failure modes injected by chaos tools:

items.text: Process kill.
Terminate a service instance randomly. Does the load balancer detect the failure and route around it within the acceptable SLA?
Network partition.
Block traffic between two services. Does Service A's circuit breaker open? Does it fail fast or queue requests indefinitely?
Latency injection.
Add 2000ms to all responses from Service B. Does Service A time out correctly? Does it cascade the slowness upstream?
Resource exhaustion.
Fill the disk, exhaust the memory, or pin the CPU of a service instance. Do health checks detect and evict the instance?
Data corruption.
Inject malformed event payloads into the message broker. Does the consumer's dead letter queue catch them? Does it alert?

runs.text: Tooling landscape: Chaos Monkey (Netflix, JVM process kill), Chaos Toolkit (open-source, declarative experiments), Gremlin (SaaS, broad failure library), LitmusChaos (Kubernetes-native, CNCF), AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS). The Resilience chapter (Chapter 5) covers the patterns these tests validate — circuit breakers, bulkheads, retries with backoff.

Run chaos experiments in production only after running them in staging. Start with the smallest possible blast radius: one instance of one non-critical service, with an abort button and an on-call engineer watching dashboards. Chaos without observability is just outage practice.

Chaos testing deliberately breaks things in a controlled way to find resilience gaps before an actual outage does. You pick a hypothesis ("the system stays up if Service B dies"), inject the failure, and observe whether you were right.

cards.title: Putting the Pyramid Together — A Testing Strategy
cards.teaser: A coherent microservices testing strategy allocates tests to the right layer, owns the flakiness budget, keeps E2E tests small, and wires every layer into the CI/CD pipeline with the appropriate gate.

runs.text: A testing strategy is not a list of what tests exist — it is a set of deliberate decisions about which tests catch which failures, how fast they run, who owns them, and what triggers them.
Recommended allocation per service:

items.text: Unit tests: 60-70% of test count.
Run on every commit. Target: under 30 seconds. Gate: required to pass before merge.
Integration tests: 15-20%.
Run on every commit with Testcontainers. Target: under 3 minutes. Gate: required to pass before merge.
Contract tests: 10-15%.
Run on every commit (consumer side) and on every provider build. Gate: required;
can-i-deploy
blocks promotion if not verified.
Component tests: 5-10%.
Run on every merge to main. Target: under 5 minutes per service. Gate: required before staging deploy.
E2E tests: fewer than 20 total across the system.
Run on merge to main against staging. Target: under 15 minutes. Gate: advisory (failures create tickets, do not always block).

runs.text: The flakiness budget is a team policy: any test that flakes more than 1% of the time is quarantined (removed from the required gate) and repaired within one sprint. Flaky required tests destroy the feedback loop — developers start ignoring failures.

The strategy is a living document. Revisit it quarterly. As the system matures, the unit/integration ratio shifts — more contract and component tests, fewer ad-hoc E2E tests added "just to be safe." The E2E suite should shrink over time, not grow.

A testing strategy is knowing which tests belong at which layer, how fast each layer should run, and what gate each layer controls in the pipeline. The goal is maximum confidence from the fastest tests possible — keeping E2E tests small and using contract and component tests for most of the heavy lifting.
